texts.fc40f1c29727:
Objective for processing:  
The data request is in support of mixed method evaluation of London Hyperacute Stroke system (HASU) and provision of 24/7 care funded by NIHR Health Services & Delivery Research Programme.
The applicant will analyse HES data and linked ONS mortality data to examine whether performance of selected clinical process is influenced by day of admission, other inputs and the extent to which patterns of provision in hours and our of hours are reflected in patient outcomes, including mortality, length of stay and patient function.
Processing activities: 
The data requested will feed into regression models as independent variables (e.g. date of admission, location and time period), dependent variables (e.g. length of stay, mortality and discharge destination) and control variables (e.g. type of stroke, procedures received, and patient demographics age, sex, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status).
Specific outputs expected, including target date:
One product of the evaluation will be the report to the funder. To ensure national and international dissemination of the learning from this proposed research, the applicant will aim to publish their findings in high impact peer reviewed journals. Data used in any of these publications will be fully anonymised and presented at an aggregate level. The applicant will also distribute accessible summaries of their work, including through online bulletins and regular updates on the project website.
In tandem with development of peer reviewed publications, the project will present its findings to national and international scientific meetings and conferences. The accessible summaries of the publications will be produced for wider dissemination to organisations including the European Stroke Organisation Conference, the Health Services Research Network symposium, the UK Stroke Forum, and the International Forum on Quality & Safety in Healthcare. They will also present findings to local stakeholders, including the London Stroke Clinical Leadership Group and the HASUs themselves.
The research will be not used to establish a protocol for a clinical trial.
The results will show the difference of patient outcomes with respect to day of admission on the aggregate level; none indicators showing the performance of an organisation will be produced.
Target dates:
Summaries and preliminary reports – by December  2015
Report to the funder – by August 2016
Journal publications – by December 2017
The data will not be used for any commercial purpose.
Outputs will contain only aggregate level data with small numbers suppressed in line with the HES analysis guide.
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date:
The proposed analysis forms part of a study that aims use qualitative and quantitative methods to evaluate the London Hyperacute Stroke system (HASU) and provision of 24/7 care and, in doing so, identify lessons about the development, provision, effects and cost of 24/7 stroke care in the London HASU system. These lessons will be of potential value to people who commission, organise and run stroke services (as described in the outputs section, above) – both in London and across any area of the English NHS that seeks to develop or provide 24/7 hyperacute stroke care. This to be delivered in December 2015, though this will be the first draft of the data. The work on the results will continue beyond this date through 2016 and 2017, as the journal publications are planned for the end of 2017. Data retention is predominantly needed to ensure that estimated results are robust and to address possible comments and suggestions of the referees.
Based on this analysis, the research aims to identify lessons that support high quality 24/7 care in a range of healthcare settings.
The applicant expects the findings from the study will lead to;
•	Improvement in patient outcomes and satisfaction for stroke patients as examples of good practice are disseminated
•	Savings in costs of care for stroke patients across the whole stroke pathway
•	Adoption of similar models across other services providing 24/7 care
•	New national guidance for standards of care for stroke patients
•	Identify areas of potential future analysis, including the impact on outcomes, patient and staff satisfaction of tailoring clinical services around the patient, for example therapy provision in the evenings and at weekends.
